profile.reading: This H5 Data Centers facility is located at 2600 West Germann Road, Chandler, Arizona 85286, in the Phoenix metro area. The operator own facility page describes a 180,000 square foot purpose built colocation building with 26 MW of capacity and up to 20 watts per cabinet density, N+1 UPS power, 48 hour diesel runtime generator backup, and N+1 cooling. The page states SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 compliance and a 100 percent uptime track record since construction. A June 29, 2023 H5 Data Centers press release documents a Phase Three expansion at this Chandler, Arizona facility, adding 30,000 square feet and 530 customer cabinets with up to 6 additional critical megawatts, bringing the campus to its current 180,000 square feet and up to 26 megawatts of IT load. H5's CEO, Josh Simms, is quoted in that release citing Arizona's attractive power costs and the state's data center sales and use tax incentive program as drivers of enterprise colocation demand in Phoenix. The release also describes the facility as a waterless Tier III design supporting power densities exceeding 20 kilowatts per cabinet. H5 Data Centers is a privately held US colocation and wholesale data center operator with facilities spanning roughly two dozen markets nationwide, per the company's own site. H5 is not a publicly traded company and does not file SEC disclosures, so this entry's specifications are sourced to the operator's own published facility page and its own press release rather than an independently audited source, a limitation this registry notes rather than treats as disqualifying, consistent with its general practice for privately held colocation operators. No year opened date was located for the original building. Arizona's data center sales and use tax exemption program, administered by the Arizona Commerce Authority, waives state and local sales tax on qualifying data center equipment purchases for certified operators, a policy H5's own Phase Three announcement cites among the incentives supporting continued Chandler expansion.

reading.body:
H5 Phoenix in Chandler, Arizona has 26 megawatts of capacity in a 180,000 square foot facility, meaning roughly 144 watts of power per square foot of built space.

This density tells you something about the building's design choices. Twenty watts per cabinet is a high-density specification, which requires careful management of cooling and power distribution to avoid hotspots. The N+1 redundancy in both UPS systems and cooling means the facility maintains full operation if any single component fails, a requirement that drives up the building's physical footprint relative to theoretical minimum capacity. The 48-hour diesel backup indicates the operator expects grid interruptions or instability long enough to matter operationally.

For AI workloads specifically, the constraint here is not raw megawatts per unit area but the ability to sustain consistent power delivery under load. SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 certifications indicate the operator monitors performance over time and meets security standards, but they do not specify the actual outage record or power quality metrics that would determine suitability for training runs. A 100 percent uptime claim since construction is notable if true, though the data does not show when construction occurred or what "uptime" excludes.

The data does not include current utilization, lease rates, or whether capacity is available. It also does not explain why this specific facility in Phoenix was built to this capacity, or whether the grid in Chandler can reliably supply 26 megawatts continuous.
